title: Design for what screens want
principle: Frank Chimero’s What Screens Want: screens are a material whose grain is flux—the capacity for change. Native screen craft manages movement, transformation, and changing data rather than dressing interfaces in skeuomorphic costumes. Designing for screens is choreography of change as much as composition of layouts.
procedure: Name the flux: what must change on this screen (data, state, navigation, time)?
Center the design on expressing that change clearly—animation only when it communicates relationships.
Treat the screen as a soft material: prefer flexible type and layout over fake physical objects.
Cut skeuomorphic/AI chrome that fights flux (static costumes, glass toys, fake paper).
Cross-check with The Web’s Grain: choices should swing with what HTML/CSS make easy and resilient.
examplePrompts:
Apply Frank Chimero’s What Screens Want honesty pass:
- Center the design on what changes (states/data), not on faux materials.
- Replace skeuomorphic/AI chrome with typographic hierarchy + clear states.
- Keep nesting only where it clarifies.
- Empty/loading/error must be plainspoken.
Return cuts + state map.
This UI uses glass cards and fake paper tear edges. Rebuild as an honest screen: ink/paper tokens, hairlines, explicit empty state.
promptWhy: Directly attacks skeuomorphic AI tells while pointing at Quiet Folio alternatives.
tips: Screens don’t care what pixels look like—they want things to move/change (Chimero).
Companion essay The Web’s Grain extends flux to web-native humility.
Keep Quiet Folio paper/ink if applying on this desk—no purple chrome.

workedExamples.title: Fake material → honest state
workedExamples.before: Leather-texture notebook UI with no clear edit state.
workedExamples.after: Paper/ink surface; explicit editing vs reading modes; fluid type measure.
workedExamples.body: Chimero: flux is the grain of screens; skeuomorphs are container costumes. Lean into change (sorts, states, transitions that explain) over leather/glass drag. Cite 2013 essay.

workedExamples.title: Quiet Folio alignment
workedExamples.body: This catalog’s letterpress desk is a metaphor worn lightly (folios, rules)—not a skeuomorphic printing press simulator.

workedExamples.title: Honest empty states
workedExamples.body: Screens want truth about emptiness. ‘No techniques match’ beats an illustration that hides the lack.

antiPatterns: Ornament that doesn’t change with data.

stateRequirements.responsive: Check 390px and desktop plus 200% zoom; preserve reading order, wrap long text and keep actions reachable.
stateRequirements.accessibility: Use semantic headings and native controls, visible labels and focus; normal text contrast at least 4.5:1.
stateRequirements.keyboard: Complete the primary action using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and Space; no pointer-only information or focus trap.
stateRequirements.reducedMotion: Remove nonessential movement; preserve all state and information without waiting for animation.
stateRequirements.loading: Show pending feedback only during real work; retain context and allow navigation away.
stateRequirements.empty: Distinguish no content from no matching results; explain how to proceed or reset filters.
stateRequirements.error: Explain the failed action, retain user input and offer recovery; never claim success on failure.
stateRequirements.interruption: A newer action wins; cancel or ignore stale results and keep controls responsive.
stateRequirements.stateChange: Announce important results politely without moving focus unexpectedly.

compatibility.rule: Start with one technique. Add at most one companion for a distinct unsolved problem; candidates are suggestions, not verified compatibility.
conflicts: Two techniques changing the same visual role require an explicit winner.
Do not combine multiple entrance or attention effects on one target.
Aesthetic subtraction must not remove semantics, feedback or attribution.
compatibility.stop: Stop when the named task is clearer and acceptance evidence is recorded; do not add polish without a problem.
